lead: A four-cylinder engine does not fire all its cylinders at once. It fires them one after another in a fixed sequence, so the power pulses arrive at equal intervals and the crankshaft is not hammered to one side. That sequence is the firing order. Related choices fix where the valves sit — the valve layout — and how they are pushed open — the valve actuation. Together these three decide how smoothly an engine runs, how well it breathes, and how much service it needs.
prereq: You need the four-stroke cycle from Chapter 1.3 and the terms lead, lag and overlap from Chapter 1.5.

blocks.text: The firing order is the sequence in which the cylinders of a multi-cylinder engine take turns to produce a power stroke. Cylinders are numbered from the front of the engine, the radiator or fan end, and cylinder 1 is the reference. The order is not a free choice: in a four-stroke engine each cylinder needs two crankshaft revolutions to finish its cycle, the pistons share crank throws, and the intake and exhaust ports must be grouped sensibly.
The angle between two successive firings, measured at the crankshaft, is the firing interval. Splitting one full cycle equally among the cylinders gives:

blocks.where: θ_f is the firing interval in crank degrees; 720 is the number of crank degrees in one four-stroke cycle (two revolutions); n is the number of cylinders. For a two-stroke the same reasoning gives 360 / n, because its cycle lasts one revolution.

blocks.text: For an inline four-cylinder engine θ_f = 720/4 = 180°. Two orders are common:

items: 1-3-4-2 — the usual order in inline four-cylinder car engines.
1-2-4-3 — the alternative; the interval is still 180°, but the two cylinders of a piston pair fire in the opposite sequence.

blocks.text: Even spacing keeps the torque reaching the crankshaft steady. It spreads the load on the main bearings, so the shaft winds and unwinds less and the engine runs quieter. The order also decides which exhaust pulses meet inside the manifold, and so how well the cylinders scavenge. Fitting spark plug leads in the wrong sequence keeps the 180° interval but scrambles the order, and the engine runs rough or will not start.
The valve layout says where the valves sit relative to the cylinder: in the block beside it, or in a head above it. Four lettered layouts name the classic arrangements.

In the L-head (flathead, or side-valve) both valves sit in the block on one side of the cylinder, and the combustion chamber extends sideways over them. One low camshaft drives them directly, so the engine is cheap and compact; this layout was common in early cars and small stationary engines. Its weakness is a long, thin chamber: the flame has far to travel, compression must stay low, and output is knock-limited.

In the T-head the valves sit one on each side of the cylinder and two camshafts are needed. In the F-head one valve is in the head and the other in the block. Both tried to improve breathing while keeping the drive simple; both are now only historical.

The I-head puts both valves in the head directly above the piston, giving a compact chamber, short flame travel and good gas flow. Almost every modern engine uses it. Its family names describe the drive: OHV (overhead valve) keeps the camshaft in the block and pushes through pushrods; OHC (overhead camshaft) puts the camshaft in the head; DOHC (double overhead camshaft) uses one camshaft for the intake valves and one for the exhaust valves, which is what makes four valves per cylinder practical.

blocks.text: Valve actuation is the chain of parts that turns crankshaft rotation into valve lift at the correct instant. Each valve opens once in two crank revolutions, so the camshaft that operates it turns at half crank speed:

blocks.where: N_cam is the camshaft speed in rev/min and N_crank is the crankshaft speed in rev/min, for a four-stroke engine. A two-stroke camshaft turns at crank speed.

items: The crankshaft drives the camshaft through gears, a chain or a toothed belt.
A cam lobe on the shaft lifts a follower as it rotates.
In a pushrod engine the follower raises a pushrod, which swings a rocker arm, which opens the valve.
In an overhead camshaft engine the lobe presses directly on a bucket over the valve.
A spring returns the valve and keeps the follower pressed against the cam.

blocks.text: Gears suit engines where the camshaft sits close to the crankshaft and last longest. Chains are durable but noisier. Toothed belts are quiet and cheap but must be replaced at a stated interval, and a snapped belt usually bends valves. Pushrods add reciprocating mass, which limits safe speed, but keep the engine compact and cheap. Overhead camshafts remove the pushrods and allow higher speeds and multi-valve heads; a rocker arm may survive as a roller finger follower. A hydraulic lifter is a small oil-filled cylinder in the valvetrain that changes length to hold the clearance at zero, so no periodic tappet adjustment is needed. Variable valve timing, the recent addition, rotates the camshaft slightly relative to the crank or switches to another cam profile; all the parts above stay in place.

figure.caption: Four power strokes of 180° crank each, starting at 0°, 180°, 360° and 540° in the order 1-3-4-2, so the engine gets one power pulse every half turn of the crank.

examples.question: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine fires in the order 1-3-4-2 and runs at 2400 rpm. Find the firing interval in crank degrees and the time between two successive firings.
steps: Firing interval: θ_f = 720 / n = 720 / 4 = 180° of crank rotation.
Convert engine speed to revolutions per second: N = 2400 / 60 = 40 rev/s.
180° is half a revolution, so the time between firings is t = 0.5 rev / 40 rev/s.
examples.answer: The firing interval is 180° of crankshaft rotation, and successive firings are 12.5 ms apart.
examples.check:
n = 4
rpm = 2400
interval = 720 / n
rev_per_s = rpm / 60
t = (interval / 360) / rev_per_s
print(interval)
print(t * 1000)

traps: For a four-stroke use 720/n for the firing interval, not 360/n. Writing 360/n is the commonest slip and loses the whole numerical mark.
Firing order and firing interval are different things. Changing the order does not change the interval for a given n; it changes balance, manifold grouping and crankshaft loading.
Cylinder numbering is a convention. State that cylinder 1 is at the front (radiator end) before using any order, because makers number differently.
L-head means both valves in the block on one side; I-head means both in the head. T-head has one on each side and F-head one in each place. Examiners test these letters.
The half-speed rule for the camshaft holds for a four-stroke only. In a two-stroke the camshaft (if fitted) turns at crank speed.

quiz.a: The firing order is the fixed sequence in which the cylinders of a multi-cylinder engine produce their power strokes, for example 1-3-4-2 in an inline four.

quiz.q: Why is the firing interval of a four-stroke engine 720/n and not 360/n?
quiz.a: A four-stroke cylinder finishes one cycle in two crank revolutions, which is 720°. Dividing 720° equally among n cylinders gives the angle between successive firings. The value 360/n would apply to a two-stroke, which fires once per revolution.

quiz.q: A six-cylinder four-stroke engine runs at 3000 rpm. Find the firing interval in crank degrees and the time between successive firings.
quiz.a: θ_f = 720/6 = 120°. Speed = 3000/60 = 50 rev/s. 120° is one third of a revolution, so t = (1/3)/50 = 0.00667 s ≈ 6.67 ms.

quiz.q: Two inline four-cylinder engines use the orders 1-3-4-2 and 1-2-4-3. The firing interval is 180° in both. What actually differs?
quiz.a: The interval and the piston pairs are identical. The order decides which cylinder of a pair fires first, so exhaust pulses reach the manifold in a different sequence and intake port pairing changes. That alters scavenging, manifold tuning and crankshaft torsional excitation, but not the interval.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of the L-head layout compared with the I-head.
quiz.a: Advantage: both valves are in the block, so one low camshaft drives them directly and the engine is cheap and compact. Disadvantage: the chamber stretches sideways over the valves, giving long flame travel, low knock-limited compression and poor breathing.

quiz.q: What is the job of a hydraulic lifter?
quiz.a: It uses oil pressure to hold the valve clearance at zero automatically, so the valvetrain stays quiet and no periodic tappet adjustment is needed.

quiz.q: A four-stroke engine runs at 2400 rpm. Find the camshaft speed and the number of times one valve opens in a minute.
quiz.a: N_cam = 2400/2 = 1200 rpm. Each valve opens once per two crank revolutions, that is once per camshaft revolution, so it opens 1200 times per minute.

quiz.q: Why does a four-valve-per-cylinder engine almost always use DOHC instead of a single overhead camshaft?
quiz.a: Four valves sit in two rows with different spacing and direction. One camshaft would need extra rocker arms to reach both rows, adding mass and friction. With two camshafts each lobe presses directly on a bucket over its own valve, and intake and exhaust timing can later be varied independently.

beyond: Not for the exam. Camshaft phasers and switchable cam profiles now appear on ordinary passenger cars sold in India, and they build directly on the belt-and-camshaft chain described here. Cylinder deactivation uses collapsing lifters to stop the valves of some cylinders under light load. Desmodromic and pneumatic valvetrains drop the return spring for very high engine speeds. Terms to search next: cam phaser, roller finger follower, lost motion, valvetrain dynamics.
